<ConflictType>Complementary information — The retrieved documents provide different but non-contradictory answers about the Great Wall's endpoints, depending on historical period and directional perspective.

The evidence clusters by historical scope and direction: d4, d6, and d7 state the Ming-era endpoints are Jiayu Pass (west) and Shanhai Pass (east) [d4, d6, d7]. d2, d3, and d5 specify the eastern end at Laolongtou/Shanhaiguan where the wall meets the sea [d2, d3, d5], while d1 and d8 mention the locations Qinhuangdao and Jiayuguan [d1, d8]. These are complementary, as they describe different aspects (east vs. west, specific landmark vs. general pass) without contradiction.

The combined evidence shows the question has multiple valid answers. The eastern end is commonly identified at Shanhaiguan/Laolongtou where the wall meets the Bohai Sea [d2, d3, d5, d6], while the western end is Jiayu Pass in Gansu [d4, d6, d8]. Source d7 clarifies that the Ming Dynasty wall ended at Hushan, indicating the answer depends on the historical period referenced.

The Great Wall has different endpoints depending on the historical period and direction considered. For the Ming Dynasty (1368–1644), the wall is often described as running from Jiayu Pass (Jiayuguan) in the west to Shanhai Pass (Shanhaiguan) in the east [d4, d6, d7]. At its eastern terminus, the wall meets the sea at a section called Laolongtou (Old Dragon's Head) near Qinhuangdao [d2, d3, d5]. Therefore, the wall's end is not a single location but varies by era and directional perspective.
